snip.t: Fundoscopy: Is there hypertensive retinopathy? — Presence of AV nicking, haemorrhages, papilloedema
Fundoscopy: Hypertensive retinopathy (A-V nipping, haemorrhages, papilloedema in malignant hypertension)
Fundoscopy reveals bilateral flame-shaped haemorrhages and papilloedema.
Papilloedema on fundoscopy or focal neurological deficits
Fundoscopy: Papilloedema (raised intracranial pressure), choroidoretinitis (e.g., ocular toxoplasmosis), retinal haemorrhages (e.g., severe malaria).
Fundoscopy – hypertensive retinopathy, diabetic retinopathy: Microvascular disease parallels renal microangiopathy.
Fundoscopy (or retinal photography): Diabetic retinopathy — Microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates

qs.q: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes presents with blurred vision. Fundoscopy reveals no retinal lesions, but the lens is cloudy. Which metabolic change in the lens epithelium most directly explains this finding?
o: Accumulation of sorbitol due to aldose reductase activity
Increased glucose uptake via SGLT2 transporter activity
Depletion of glutathione due to elevated oxidative stress
Conversion of fructose to sorbitol via dehydrogenase action
Inhibition of hexokinase through high glucose concentration
qs.e: Excess glucose is converted to sorbitol, which accumulates in the lens, causing osmotic swelling and cataracts.

qs.q: A 70-year-old male with Waldenström Macroglobulinemia presents with sudden vision loss and epistaxis. Fundoscopy shows 'sausage-link' retinal veins. Serum viscosity is 4.5 centipoise. What is the immediate treatment?
qs.e: Hyperviscosity syndrome is a medical emergency. Plasmapheresis rapidly removes the excess IgM paraprotein, immediately reducing serum viscosity and reversing symptoms. Rituximab is used later for disease control.
qs.s: Advanced Haematology & Transfusion Medicine Cases Exam Prep
